name: Acetabular labral tear
populations: women with hip dysplasia or hypermobility
athletes in pivoting, kicking and end-range sports
summary: Detachment or splitting of the fibrocartilaginous rim of the hip socket, usually anterosuperior, causing groin pain and clicking. Often secondary to FAI morphology or dysplasia and common without symptoms.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: At least 3 months of exercise-based care; 4–9 months after arthroscopic repair

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: FADIR: high sensitivity, poor specificity; a negative test helps rule out intra-articular pain

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: 3 T MRI or MR arthrography (Sn ≈0.80–0.89, Sp ≈0.69–0.77)

keyFacts.label: Site
keyFacts.value: Anterosuperior quadrant in about three-quarters of tears

keyFacts.label: Caution
keyFacts.value: Labral tears are seen on MRI in about half of people without hip pain

keyFacts.label: Diagnostic delay
keyFacts.value: Mean 21 months from symptom onset in one surgical series

grading: Histological tear type (Seldes)

keywords.mechanism: Most labral tears result from repetitive loading of the anterosuperior rim: in FAI the femoral head–neck junction shears or crushes the labrum in flexion and internal rotation; in dysplasia the labrum is overloaded as the femoral head translates toward the shallow rim [r7]. An acute tear typically occurs during a forceful twist or pivot on a loaded, flexed hip, a slip into hyperabduction, or end-range hip extension with external rotation, which increases anterior joint force [r8].

name: Achilles tendon rupture
summary: A complete tear of the Achilles tendon, usually in the mid-portion, from a sudden push-off or forced dorsiflexion in a degenerate tendon. It causes a pop, weak push-off and a palpable gap.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Function returns over 6–12 months; calf strength and size deficits can persist beyond a year

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: 80% return to play (95% CI 75–85%) in a meta-analysis, usually after 6–12 months; criteria-based

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Calf squeeze (Thompson) test: Sn 96%, Sp 93%; Matles Sn 88%, Sp 85%

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not needed if the clinical tests are clearly positive; ultrasound or MRI if uncertain, partial or chronic

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Mean age about 45 in a Danish registry; men three times as often as women

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: About 27–31 per 100,000 per year in Denmark (1994–2013), rising in people over 50

grading: Descriptive classification (no universally accepted grading scale)

keywords.mechanism: Most ruptures are non-contact and happen during an explosive push-off: forward acceleration from standing, cross-over cutting or jumping [r2]. At the injury frame in professional footballers the ankle was at end-range dorsiflexion (about 40°), the hip extended and the trunk slightly flexed, with the knee near extension or early flexion (about 22°) and the foot pronated [r2]. The calf contracts forcefully against a tendon that is being lengthened, and the load exceeds the capacity of a degenerate mid-portion [r1].

name: Acute adductor longus strain
summary: An acute tear of the adductor longus at its proximal tendon, musculotendinous junction or pubic insertion, caused by rapid activation while the muscle is being rapidly lengthened in kicking or change of direction.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Median ~18 days to full training for MRI grade 0–2; ~11 weeks for complete tears/avulsions

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based; being clinically pain-free before return is linked to fewer reinjuries

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Palpation of the proximal adductor longus plus resisted adduction (squeeze) reproducing the injury pain

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI only if a complete tear/avulsion is suspected or for prognosis in elite sport

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Young adults (median 27 years in an MRI cohort)

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: ~70% non-contact: change of direction, kicking, reaching, jumping

grading: MRI grading 0–3 (used in the Aspetar adductor cohort studies)

structures: Proximal adductor longus tendon and pubic enthesis
Adductor brevis, pectineus and obturator externus
Adductor longus MTJs (proximal or distal tendon)
Proximal adductor longus tendon / pubic enthesis
differentials: Hip-related groin pain (FAI syndrome / labral tear)
keywords.mechanism: Video analysis of acute adductor longus injuries in professional football found that 71% were non-contact and that more than half followed a quick reaction to a change in play [r4]. The injuring actions were change of direction (35%), kicking (29%), reaching (24%) and jumping (12%). Closed-chain injuries (change of direction, reaching) occurred with the hip extended, abducted and externally rotated. Open-chain injuries (kicking, jumping) occurred as the hip moved from extension to flexion and from abduction to adduction [r4]. The common thread is rapid muscle activation during rapid lengthening. In a maximal kick the adductor longus is lengthening fastest (~22 cm/s) near peak hip extension at about 40% of swing, just as it is activating to drive the limb forward [r5].

name: Acute hamstring strain
populations: older athletes with a previous hamstring injury
summary: A tear of the hamstring muscle fibres, usually the biceps femoris long head near its proximal musculotendinous junction, during high-speed running or an extreme hip-flexion stretch.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Sprint-type 2–8 weeks; stretch-type or intratendinous injuries take much longer

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based: pain-free palpation, strength, flexibility and maximal sprinting

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Palpation (site and length of tenderness) plus resisted knee flexion; Askling H-test before RTS

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not routine. MRI if avulsion is suspected, in elite athletes, or for recurrent injury

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 22% of elite male footballers per season

keyFacts.label: Recurrence
keyFacts.value: 13.9–63.3% within 2 years

grading: British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification (BAMIC)

keywords.mechanism: Sprint-type HSI occurs at maximal running speed, most often in late swing. The hip is flexed and the knee extends rapidly as the shank swings forward. The biarticular hamstrings contract eccentrically to decelerate the shank, so they are long, highly active and lengthening at their peak velocity [r10]. The long head of biceps femoris fails, typically near its proximal musculotendinous junction (MTJ) [r2]. Stretch-type HSI happens during slow, extreme hip flexion with the knee extended and usually affects the proximal semimembranosus tendon [r3].

name: Acute non-specific low back pain (muscle/ligament strain)
populations: people with previous episodes of low back pain
desk-based workers with long sitting exposure
summary: Back pain of under 6 weeks with no identifiable structural cause, usually triggered by a loaded or awkward movement. It improves quickly in most people, but recurs often and is shaped by biopsychosocial factors.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Mean pain falls from 52 to 23 (0–100 scale) by 6 weeks, then improves more slowly

keyFacts.label: Recurrence
keyFacts.value: 69% have another episode within 12 months

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: No test identifies the painful tissue; screen for red flags and for radicular signs

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not routinely needed: immediate imaging did not improve outcomes in 6 trials (n = 1804)

keyFacts.label: Serious pathology
keyFacts.value: 0.9% (11 of 1172) in one primary care cohort; 8 of the 11 were fractures

keyFacts.label: Burden
keyFacts.value: Leading cause of disability worldwide

grading: Duration-based classification (conventional) and prognostic risk

tests: Straight leg raise or slump test (screen for radicular involvement)
structures: Lumbar nerve roots and dorsal rami
Interspinous and supraspinous ligaments and facet capsules
differentials: Vertebral fracture, infection, malignancy or inflammatory back pain
keywords.mechanism: Most acute episodes are triggered, not caused by one identifiable injury. In a case-crossover study of 999 people with sudden-onset LBP, brief exposures in the 2 hours before onset (manual tasks with heavy loads, awkward postures, caring for live people or animals, moderate or vigorous activity and fatigue during a task) increased the odds of an episode 2.9 to 11.7 times [r7]. The painful tissue is rarely demonstrable, so the animation shows a provocative loaded bend and then the whole set of candidate tissues rather than one failing structure.

name: Adductor-related groin pain (longstanding)
summary: Longstanding groin pain from the adductor longus origin (adductor tenderness plus pain on resisted adduction) that builds up in kicking and cutting sports and responds to progressive adductor strengthening.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: 8–12 weeks of progressive active training, then graded return

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: 79% returned to the same level without groin pain after active training

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Adductor longus origin palpation + resisted adduction (squeeze) reproducing pain

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Rarely needed. MRI changes are common in asymptomatic footballers

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Most common groin entity: 61% of athletes in a groin clinic

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Cumulative kicking, cutting and skating load exceeding adductor capacity

structures: Adductor longus enthesis and proximal tendon
differentials: Hip-related groin pain (FAI syndrome / labral tear)
Obturator nerve entrapment / referred lumbar pain
keywords.mechanism: ARGP develops when the cumulative load at the adductor longus origin outpaces its capacity to adapt. Each kick, side-step, reach or skating stride loads the adductor eccentrically at long length and transmits force across the anterior pubis. This happens through an aponeurotic connection with the contralateral rectus sheath, the symphysis capsule and the opposite adductor longus [r8]. Pain usually starts as stiffness after training and progresses to pain during sport, especially with sudden increases in match or training load [r4,r6].

name: Anterior ankle impingement
summary: Anterior ankle pain and limited dorsiflexion from bone spurs or thickened soft tissue pinched at end-range dorsiflexion, common in footballers, dancers and after repeated sprains.

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Recurrent (hyper)dorsiflexion and repetitive microtrauma to the anterior ankle

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Conservative care first. After arthroscopy, 74–100% satisfaction in a systematic review; full activity at about 5–10 weeks in one older series

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Anterior joint-line tenderness with pain and a hard end-feel on forced dorsiflexion (clinical diagnosis)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Lateral plus oblique anteromedial radiographs: sensitivity for tibial osteophytes 85% vs 40% on a lateral view alone

keyFacts.label: Typical patient
keyFacts.value: Active adult; average age 31 years in a surgical cohort of 62 patients

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based; pain-free loading into end-range dorsiflexion

grading: Osteoarthritis and impingement classification used in arthroscopy studies

structures: Anterior tibial lip and talar neck
differentials: Stress fracture of the anterior tibia or talus
keywords.mechanism: Repeated forced dorsiflexion drives the anterior tibial lip down onto the talar neck. At about 15° of dorsiflexion a triangular synovial and fat-collagen soft tissue component in the anterior joint is squeezed between the tibia and talus [r3]. Over time repetitive microtrauma, such as ball impact on the anteromedial ankle in kickers [r4], and abnormal soft tissue thickening after earlier injury produce spurs and a thickened capsule or synovium, which block end-range dorsiflexion [r2]. The exact cause of the spurs remains debated [r3,r4].

name: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture
summary: A partial or complete tear of the ACL, usually from a non-contact deceleration, landing or cutting movement with the knee near extension and collapsing into valgus.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: 9–12 months after reconstruction; rehab-first pathway 3–6 months to stable function

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Not before 9 months post-reconstruction and only once criteria are met

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Lachman (Sn 85%, Sp 94%); pivot shift (Sp 98%)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI confirms and identifies associated meniscal, chondral and bone injuries

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: 15–25 years

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: ~70% non-contact

grading: Anatomical sprain grade (with instrumented / clinical laxity)

structures: Lateral femoral condyle & posterolateral tibial plateau
keywords.mechanism: The classic non-contact ACL rupture happens about 40 ms after initial foot contact during a deceleration, side-step cut or one-leg landing. The knee is only slightly flexed (≈20–30°) and collapses into valgus coupled with internal tibial rotation while ground-reaction forces peak at about three times body weight [r3]. A strong quadriceps contraction near extension adds anterior tibial shear, which the ACL must resist [r2].

name: Anterior shoulder dislocation (with Bankart/Hill–Sachs)
summary: The humeral head is forced forward out of the glenoid, usually in abduction, external rotation and extension, tearing the anteroinferior labrum (Bankart) and often denting the humeral head (Hill–Sachs).

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Rehabilitation over about 3–6 months; after surgical stabilisation about 6 months before contact sport (clinical convention)

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based, not before about 3 months after non-operative care or about 6 months after stabilisation

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Relocation test (LR+ 6.5) and anterior release test (LR+ 8.3)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Radiographs before and after reduction; MRI or MR arthrography for labrum and cuff; CT for bone loss

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: 20–29 years; 71.8% of emergency department cases are male

keyFacts.label: Recurrence
keyFacts.value: About 39% overall in adults; markedly higher at 40 years or under

grading: Patterns of structural injury (descriptive; there is no validated grading)

tests: Deltoid isometric contraction and regimental badge sensation
keywords.mechanism: The classic mechanism is a force that drives an abducted, externally rotated arm further into external rotation and extension, such as an arm tackle, a fall onto the outstretched or abducted arm, or a forced throw. The humeral head levers over the anteroinferior glenoid rim, tears the anterior capsulolabral complex and comes to rest forward of and below the coracoid. The posterolateral head impacts the glenoid rim on the way, producing a Hill–Sachs impaction.

name: Articular cartilage (chondral/osteochondral) defect of the knee
populations: people after ACL injury or patellar dislocation
summary: A focal loss of articular (hyaline) cartilage, with or without underlying bone, from impaction, shear or chronic overload. It causes activity-related pain and effusion and has very limited capacity to heal.

keyFacts.label: Prevalence
keyFacts.value: Chondral lesions in ~60% of knee arthroscopies; full-thickness defects in 36% of athletes

keyFacts.label: Healing
keyFacts.value: Hyaline cartilage is avascular and has almost no intrinsic capacity to heal

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: No accurate clinical test; MRI with cartilage-sensitive sequences or arthroscopy confirms

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI shows depth, size and subchondral bone; radiographs for loose bodies and alignment

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: 76% after cartilage surgery; ~5 months (OAT) to ~12 months (ACI)

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: 3-month active rehab trial first; 9–18 months after cartilage repair

grading: ICRS (International Cartilage Regeneration & Joint Preservation Society) grade

keywords.mechanism: Acute defects occur when high compressive load is combined with shear: a landing or pivot on a flexed knee, the femorotibial impaction of an ACL pivot-shift, the shear of a patella dislocating and relocating, or a direct blow on a flexed knee. Chronic defects develop when repetitive load exceeds the capacity of cartilage in a joint with malalignment, instability or meniscal loss. The weight-bearing medial femoral condyle and the patella are most often affected [r2,r3].

name: Carpal tunnel syndrome
aka: median nerve compression at the wrist
populations: people in forceful, repetitive or vibratory manual work
people with diabetes, obesity or thyroid disease
summary: Compression of the median nerve in the carpal tunnel, causing night-time pain, numbness and tingling in the thumb, index and middle fingers and, in severe cases, thenar weakness. Most start with non-surgical care.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Symptoms are reviewed over weeks to 3 months with non-surgical care; surgery is considered when symptoms persist [Cochrane]

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: No single test is reliable: pooled Phalen Sn 0.57, Sp 0.67; Tinel Sn 0.45, Sp 0.78. Combine history, hand diagram and sensorimotor tests

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Nerve conduction studies (median across the wrist versus a comparison nerve segment) are the most sensitive and accurate neurophysiological test

keyFacts.label: Outcome measure
keyFacts.value: Boston Carpal Tunnel Questionnaire (symptom and function scales, 1 = best, 5 = worst)

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Trial participants were mostly middle-aged women (84% women in the surgical-versus-non-surgical Cochrane trials)

keyFacts.label: Work link
keyFacts.value: Force, repetition and vibration are associated with CTS; evidence that computer work causes it is insufficient

grading: Practical severity grouping (clinical convention, not a validated cut-off set)

structures: Digital flexor tendons and synovial sheaths
Palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve
differentials: Pronator teres syndrome or proximal median neuropathy
keywords.mechanism: CTS has no single injury moment. Carpal tunnel pressure rises when the tunnel contents (nerve, flexor tendons and their synovial lining) outgrow the space available or when sustained wrist postures and loading increase the pressure on them. The median nerve is then compressed against the tough flexor retinaculum, which forms the roof of the tunnel [r3]. Elevated pressure, ischaemia, mechanical trauma, demyelination and tenosynovial change are all proposed contributors, with mechanical factors considered most likely [r3].

name: Chronic ankle instability
populations: athletes with a previous lateral ankle sprain
summary: Recurrent giving way and sprains more than 12 months after a lateral ankle sprain, driven by lasting mechanical laxity and sensorimotor deficits rather than by one structure alone.

keyFacts.label: Definition
keyFacts.value: More than 12 months after the first sprain, with recurrent sprains, frequent giving way and persistent symptoms

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Estimates range from 10–20% (Cochrane review) to up to 40% after a first lateral ankle sprain

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Exercise-based rehabilitation is first-line; neuromuscular training improved function at 4 weeks in small trials

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: No single test: combine history of giving way, a validated questionnaire, laxity tests and balance tests

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Radiographs to exclude other causes; MRI or arthroscopy for associated cartilage and ligament lesions

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based, usually with a brace or tape and ongoing balance training

grading: Contributing-factor classification (mechanical, functional, combined)

differentials: Cavovarus foot or neuropathic cause of giving way
keywords.mechanism: CAI develops when the first lateral ankle sprain leaves lasting mechanical changes (laxity of the repaired ATFL and CFL) together with disrupted afferent input, altered reflexes and motor control, and altered perception of the ankle [r1,r12]. In later landings and cuts the foot reaches the vulnerable inverted position with a smaller trigger and a slower or poorly organised protective response, and the ankle gives way. Each event can add further capsular, cartilage and synovial damage [r10].

name: De Quervain's tenosynovitis
aka: stenosing tenosynovitis of the first dorsal compartment
populations: people in repetitive thumb and wrist work
summary: Stenosing tenosynovitis of the first dorsal compartment (APL and EPB) at the radial styloid, causing radial wrist pain with thumb use. It follows repetitive thumb and wrist loading, infant handling or wrist trauma.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Conservative care first; injection success is documented at 61–83% in a review, and a splint added to injection helps short and mid-term (moderate evidence)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Finkelstein and Eichhoff tests have low specificity; the WHAT test was proposed as an alternative. Accuracy figures were not retrieved

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Ultrasound can show the intercompartmental septum and made injections more accurate with better outcomes in a review

keyFacts.label: Risk setting
keyFacts.value: 26.8% of 190 infant caregivers had a positive Finkelstein test (small cross-sectional study)

keyFacts.label: After fracture
keyFacts.value: 2.2% (operative) to 3.8% (non-operative) of distal radius fracture patients developed it within a year

keyFacts.label: Nature of the problem
keyFacts.value: Thickening of the first dorsal compartment retinaculum with a degenerative rather than purely inflammatory histology

grading: Practical severity and duration grouping (clinical convention; no validated grading system)

tests: Wrist hyperflexion and abduction of the thumb (WHAT) test
Palpation and resisted thumb extension and abduction
differentials: Trigger thumb (flexor pollicis longus stenosing tenosynovitis)
keywords.mechanism: There is no single injury moment. Repeated or sustained thumb abduction and extension combined with wrist ulnar deviation, for example pinch gripping, lifting an infant under the arms, or racquet and tool use, drives the APL and EPB tendons to glide around the radial styloid through a tight fibro-osseous canal. Resisted gliding of these tendons in the canal produces the pain [r1]. In susceptible people the compartment roof thickens and narrows, so the friction rises and pain appears with smaller loads [r3].

name: Degenerative meniscal tear
summary: A slowly developing meniscal lesion, usually a horizontal cleavage of the medial posterior horn in people over 35, often an early feature of osteoarthritis. Exercise therapy is first-line, not arthroscopy.

keyFacts.label: First-line care
keyFacts.value: Supervised exercise therapy and education for about 12 weeks

keyFacts.label: Arthroscopy
keyFacts.value: Partial meniscectomy is no better than sham surgery or exercise; not first-line

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Weight-bearing radiographs if needed; MRI is usually not indicated first-line

keyFacts.label: Prevalence
keyFacts.value: Present on MRI in 19–56% of people aged 50–90; most are asymptomatic

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Over 35 years; most common from 50 onwards

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Improvement over 3–6 months, continuing to 2 years

grading: MRI meniscal signal grade (intrasubstance to surface tear)

keywords.mechanism: There is no significant injury. With age and cumulative compressive load, the meniscal matrix loses its organisation and strength, so a trivial movement such as rising from a squat with a small twist is enough to complete a tear. Shear stress within the wedge produces a horizontal cleavage, most often in the posterior horn of the medial meniscus, where compressive load in flexion is greatest [r1,r10].

name: Distal biceps tendon rupture
aka: biceps tendon rupture at the elbow
populations: people with a raised body mass index
summary: Acute avulsion of the distal biceps tendon from the radial tuberosity under a sudden eccentric load on a flexed elbow, causing a pop, a Popeye deformity and weak supination. Repair is usually favoured in active people.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: After repair, in a meta-analysis flexion strength reached 94.7% and supination strength 89.2% of the other arm, versus 83.0% and 62.6% without surgery

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based, set by the surgeon's protocol; lifting is typically restricted for about 3–6 months (clinical convention)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Hook test: abnormal in 33 of 33 complete avulsions and normal in 45 of 45 uninjured arms (sensitivity and specificity both 100% in one surgeon's 45-patient cohort)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not needed if the hook test is clear. MRI is used to separate partial from complete tears (sensitivity 92%, specificity 85% in the same cohort)

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Mean age about 46 years; about 95% of cases are in men

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: About 2.55 per 100,000 patient-years in a US national insurance database

grading: Clinical classification: partial versus complete rupture, with or without retraction

tests: Observation for Popeye deformity and ecchymosis
structures: Lateral antebrachial cutaneous and posterior interosseous nerves
differentials: Partial distal biceps tear or tendinopathy
Bicipitoradial bursitis or anterior elbow impingement
keywords.mechanism: Distal biceps rupture is a sudden failure of the tendon at its insertion on the radial tuberosity. The elbow is flexed and the forearm supinated with the biceps contracting to hold a heavy load. When the load exceeds what the muscle can resist, the elbow is forced towards extension and the biceps lengthens while still contracting. Every patient in a defined cohort described excessive eccentric tension as the arm was forced from a flexed position [r1]. Failure occurs in a tendon with a hypovascular zone that can be nipped between the radius and ulna in pronation, which may have weakened it beforehand [r3].

name: Distal radius fracture
populations: snow, skate and roller sport participants
people after a fall on an outstretched hand
summary: A break of the distal radius, most often from a fall on an outstretched hand; the classic Colles pattern is dorsally displaced. Common in older women and children; needs same-day imaging and a neurovascular check.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Cast or fixation then rehabilitation; most trial outcomes are measured at 12 months

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Radiographs (PA and lateral); the Lafontaine criteria flag fractures at risk of secondary displacement

keyFacts.label: Older adults
keyFacts.value: Casting is recommended for adults over 65 because long-term outcomes are similar with surgery; trade-offs exist between pain and grip and range (WRIST analyses)

keyFacts.label: Prevention (CRPS)
keyFacts.value: Vitamin C 500 mg daily for 50 days: CRPS RR 0.54 (95% CI 0.33–0.91) in a 3-trial meta-analysis

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Children and older adults carry the greatest risk; 87% of the older-adult WRIST trial participants were women

keyFacts.label: Children
keyFacts.value: Torus (buckle) fractures: a soft bandage was equivalent to rigid immobilisation for pain at 3 days (FORCE)

grading: Descriptive classification (clinical convention) and AO/OTA groups

tests: Radiographic assessment of reduction and alignment (PA and lateral views)
structures: Radial styloid and radiocarpal articular surface
Distal radioulnar joint, TFCC and ulnar styloid
Ulnar styloid and distal radioulnar joint
differentials: Distal radioulnar joint injury or Galeazzi pattern
keywords.mechanism: The classic distal radius fracture follows a fall forward on to an outstretched hand with the wrist forced into extension. The ground reaction force travels up the hand and through the carpus into the distal radius, loading the metaphysis. The volar cortex fails in tension and the fracture line runs dorsally, where compression crushes the dorsal cortex. The distal fragment is displaced and tilted dorsally with radial shortening, which gives the 'dinner-fork' deformity of the Colles pattern (clinical biomechanics).

name: Femoral neck stress fracture
aka: fatigue fracture of the femoral neck
populations: female athletes with low energy availability
summary: A fatigue fracture of the femoral neck from repetitive loading, usually in runners and recruits. Tension-side fractures can displace and cause avascular necrosis, so suspected cases need urgent MRI.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Compression-side, low grade: about 6–14 weeks; after fixation: 3–6+ months

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Graded return to running once walking and hopping are pain-free and imaging shows healing

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: No accurate clinical test; groin pain on hopping or weight-bearing should prompt MRI

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Radiographs often normal early; MRI is the definitive investigation

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: About 3% of sport-related stress fractures

keyFacts.label: Risk
keyFacts.value: High-risk site: delayed diagnosis increases displacement, AVN and career-ending outcomes

grading: Fullerton & Snowdy classification (with Kaeding–Miller grade)

differentials: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
keywords.mechanism: With each foot strike, body weight and muscle forces bend the femoral neck in the frontal plane: the inferomedial cortex is compressed and the superolateral cortex is placed in tension. Thousands of submaximal loading cycles create microdamage faster than targeted remodelling can repair it, so bone resorption temporarily exceeds formation and the neck weakens [r2,r5]. Compression-side injuries begin at the inferomedial neck; tension-side injuries start superolaterally, where crack propagation and poor healing make displacement more likely [r4].

name: Femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) syndrome
populations: male adolescent and young adult athletes
summary: Motion-related hip or groin pain caused by premature contact between the femur and acetabulum, from cam and/or pincer morphology, with positive clinical signs and imaging findings.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: At least 3 months of exercise-based care; 6–12 months after arthroscopy

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: FADIR: high sensitivity (≈94–99%), so a negative test helps rule out; it cannot confirm

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: AP pelvis + lateral (e.g. Dunn 45°) radiographs first; MRI/MRA only if it will change management

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Late adolescence to 40s; cam morphology forms before the growth plate closes

keyFacts.label: Diagnosis
keyFacts.value: Triad: symptoms + clinical signs + imaging (Warwick Agreement)

keyFacts.label: Management
keyFacts.value: Physio-led exercise first line; arthroscopy gives a modest extra short-term benefit in selected patients

grading: Morphological type (Warwick Agreement terminology)

differentials: Acetabular labral tear (without distinct bony morphology)
keywords.mechanism: FAI syndrome is a motion-driven overuse condition rather than a single injury. During hip flexion, especially when combined with adduction and internal rotation, a cam bump at the anterosuperior head–neck junction is levered into the acetabulum, or a pincer rim contacts the femoral neck early [r3,r12]. Repeated contact shears the acetabular cartilage away from the labrum (cam) or crushes the labrum between rim and neck (pincer). Symptoms appear when cumulative load exceeds the capacity of the chondrolabral tissues.

name: Frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis)
populations: people after shoulder surgery or trauma
summary: A painful, then stiff shoulder from capsular inflammation, fibrosis and contracture, with marked loss of passive external rotation. The natural history is long and variable.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Long and variable; most improvement is early, and about 4 in 10 still have mostly mild symptoms at about 4 years

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Mainly an activity problem: return as pain settles and range and strength recover

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Passive external rotation restricted by about 50% or more compared with the other side, with a normal radiograph

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Radiographs to exclude other pathology; ultrasound or MRI only if a cuff tear or other cause is suspected

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: About 40–60 years (mean onset about 53)

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Around 10% of people in their fifties; people with diabetes have about 5 times the risk

grading: Descriptive stages (freezing, frozen, thawing) — not a validated grading

tests: Passive external rotation at the side
Resisted tests and cuff screen (external rotation lag and drop-arm)
structures: Rotator interval (coracohumeral and superior glenohumeral ligaments)
Axillary recess and inferior glenohumeral ligament
Capsule and synovium of the rotator interval
keywords.mechanism: Most frozen shoulder is primary (idiopathic): there is no single injury. A chronic inflammatory and fibroblastic process develops in the glenohumeral capsule, particularly the rotator interval and axillary recess, which thickens, scars and contracts so that the joint's capacity is reduced and movement, especially external rotation, is lost. A secondary form follows trauma, surgery or immobilisation.

name: Hip (proximal femoral) fracture in older adults
populations: people with frailty, dementia or falls history
summary: A fracture of the femoral neck or trochanteric region, usually from a sideways fall onto the hip in an older adult with fragile bone. Treated with early surgery, mobilisation within 36 h and multidisciplinary rehab.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Most mobility gains in 3–6 months; many never regain pre-fracture mobility

keyFacts.label: Key priority
keyFacts.value: Surgery within 24–48 h and mobilisation within 36 h of surgery

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: AP pelvis and lateral hip radiograph; MRI if clinical suspicion persists despite normal films

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Mean about 85 years; about 75% women

keyFacts.label: Mortality
keyFacts.value: Roughly 1 in 5 die within a year; 5–8× higher risk of death in the first 3 months

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Sideways fall with impact on the greater trochanter

grading: Anatomical classification (intracapsular vs extracapsular, displacement)

structures: Soft tissues over the greater trochanter
differentials: Femoral neck stress or insufficiency fracture
Osteoporotic vertebral fracture with referred pain
Acetabular fracture or flare of hip osteoarthritis
keywords.mechanism: The typical hip fracture results from a fall directly sideways from standing height, with impact on the greater trochanter. In a prospective study of 206 consecutive hip fractures, 76% of patients fell directly to the side, 56% had a fresh haematoma over the greater trochanter, and most did not break the fall with an outstretched arm [r3]. The impact load through the trochanter bends and shears the femoral neck or trochanteric region, and osteoporotic bone fails at a load it would once have tolerated.

name: Iliopsoas strain and iliopsoas-related groin pain
summary: Anterior groin pain from the iliacus, psoas or their common tendon and bursa: an acute strain at the MTJ during sprinting or change of direction, or longstanding overload with pain on resisted hip flexion and stretch.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Acute MTJ strain ~1–4 weeks; longstanding tendon or bursal pain 6–12 weeks

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based: pain-free resisted hip flexion, stretch, sprinting and kicking

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Iliopsoas tenderness + pain on resisted hip flexion and/or hip flexor stretch (modified Thomas)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Usually not needed. MRI/US for persisting or atypical pain

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Hip flexors account for about a third of acute groin injuries

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Change of direction, sprinting and kicking: rapid hip flexion from an extended hip

differentials: Hip-related groin pain (FAI syndrome / labral tear)
keywords.mechanism: Acute iliopsoas strains occur when the muscle is loaded quickly at long length. This happens at the end of hip extension in sprinting or as the athlete brakes and pushes off to change direction, when the iliopsoas is activated eccentrically to stop extension and then concentrically to drive the thigh forward. Iliacus injuries occurred mostly during change of direction, and iliacus and psoas injuries clustered at the MTJ [r3]. Longstanding iliopsoas-related pain develops from repetitive hip flexion under load (kicking, sprinting, sit-ups, dance), which irritates the tendon and the iliopsoas bursa where they glide over the iliopectineal eminence and anterior hip capsule [r8].

name: Iliotibial band syndrome
summary: Lateral knee pain from repetitive loading of the iliotibial band over the lateral femoral epicondyle, typically in runners. It is thought to reflect compression of the tissue under the band rather than simple friction.

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Roughly 5–14% of running injuries; the most common lateral knee injury in runners

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Improvement over about 2–8 weeks of treatment in published studies; longer if long-standing

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Pain at the lateral epicondyle at ~30° knee flexion (Noble compression, single-leg squat); no validated accuracy data

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Usually not needed; MRI or ultrasound excludes other causes of lateral knee pain

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Graded return to running once pain-free with hip strength restored; no validated criteria

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Repetitive stance-phase loading with the knee near 20–30° flexion

tests: Single-leg squat or step-down with pain provocation
structures: Fat and loose connective tissue deep to the band
Tensor fasciae latae and gluteus maximus
differentials: Posterolateral corner or lateral collateral ligament injury
Osteochondritis dissecans or lateral femoral condyle bone stress injury
Gluteal tendinopathy or lateral hip pain
keywords.mechanism: ITBS has no single injury moment. It develops from thousands of repeated stance phases in which the knee is only slightly flexed. In nine runners with ITBS the knee was flexed about 21° at footstrike, and the band was thought to impinge at or just below the 30° of flexion traditionally described [r5]. In MRI of volunteers the band was compressed against the lateral epicondyle at about 30° of flexion, as a result of internal rotation of the tibia, and moved laterally off the epicondyle in extension [r3]. Greater peak hip adduction and knee internal rotation preceded ITBS in a prospective study of female runners and may increase strain in the band [r9].

name: Infrapatellar (Hoffa's) fat pad impingement
populations: young athletes in jumping and kicking sports
dancers and gymnasts with knee hyperextension
people after knee arthroscopy or ACL reconstruction
summary: Pain below the patella when the infrapatellar fat pad is pinched between the femur, tibia and patellar tendon, usually in knee hyperextension, causing inflammation, swelling and later fibrosis.

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Hyperextension or direct blow pinching the fat pad; patella alta and maltracking

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Hoffa's test and pain on passive hyperextension (no accuracy data)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Sagittal MRI shows fat pad oedema; common in asymptomatic athletes too

keyFacts.label: Evidence
keyFacts.value: No treatment trials; management is based on expert opinion and case series

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Usually settles over 6–12 weeks with unloading and exercise

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Adolescents and young adults; any age after knee surgery

structures: Femoral condyles and anterior tibial plateau
differentials: Fat pad mass or synovial tumour
keywords.mechanism: Impingement occurs when the knee moves into extension or hyperextension and the fat pad is compressed between the inferior pole of the patella, the femoral condyles and the anterior tibial plateau. A sudden forced hyperextension (kicking air, an awkward landing) or a direct blow can bruise it acutely; repetitive end-range extension, standing in recurvatum or a high-riding, laterally tracking patella pinch it repeatedly [r1,r3]. Once inflamed, the swollen fat pad is pinched more easily, creating a self-perpetuating cycle.

name: Inguinal-related groin pain ("sports hernia")
populations: kicking, sprinting and change-of-direction sport athletes
summary: Longstanding pain in the inguinal canal region with canal tenderness and no palpable hernia, typically worse with coughing, sneezing, sit-ups, sprinting and kicking. It is the Doha term for 'sports hernia'.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Rehabilitation-first for 6–12 weeks; ~73% return pain-free at about 10 weeks in rehab cohorts

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: After surgery for failed rehab, most return within 6–12 weeks

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Recognisable pain on inguinal canal palpation (scrotal invagination + Valsalva) and on resisted sit-up

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Ultrasound (dynamic) to exclude true hernia; MRI for other entities

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Mid-20s to early 30s (mean ~28 years in surgical series)

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Repetitive trunk rotation and hip extension under load: kicking, sprinting, cutting

tests: Inguinal canal palpation with Valsalva (scrotal invagination)
structures: External oblique aponeurosis and superficial ring
Ilioinguinal and genital branch of genitofemoral nerve
Adductor longus origin and rectus abdominis insertion
keywords.mechanism: IRGP is an overuse condition of the lower abdominal wall at the inguinal canal. Repetitive, forceful trunk rotation and hip extension during kicking, sprinting and cutting load the external oblique aponeurosis, the conjoint tendon and the transversalis fascia of the posterior inguinal wall. The rectus abdominis and abdominal wall pull the pubis upward while the adductors pull it downward. When this repetitive load exceeds tissue capacity, the posterior wall and aponeurosis attenuate and develop microtears, and the ilioinguinal, iliohypogastric or genitofemoral nerves can become irritated or entrapped [r3,r8].

name: Insertional Achilles tendinopathy
populations: people with a Haglund prominence or heel spur
summary: Pain, swelling and stiffness at the Achilles insertion on the back of the heel, from tensile and compressive overload against the calcaneus, often with a bursa or spur. End-range dorsiflexion loading aggravates it.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Slow: months of loading, with about two-thirds satisfied at 4 months in a pilot of modified training; surgery only after failed conservative care

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based graded return after a loading phase that avoids end-range dorsiflexion at first

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Tenderness within the distal 2 cm of the tendon at the heel, with pain on dorsiflexion and heel compression

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Lateral weight-bearing radiograph for a spur, calcification or Haglund prominence; ultrasound or MRI for tendon and bursa. Findings track symptoms poorly

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Middle-aged and older adults: mean age 53 in a loading pilot and 59 in a biomechanics study

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: About 6% of people report Achilles pain in their lifetime, and roughly one-third of that is insertional

grading: MRI grading (Nicholson and colleagues, 2007, as reported by Chimenti and colleagues) with the tendinopathy continuum for load-based staging [r1,r10]

tests: Palpation of the distal 2 cm of the tendon and retrocalcaneal region
Single-leg heel raise and hop provocation
keywords.mechanism: IAT results from combined tensile and compressive overload at the insertion. As the calf pulls, the superficial fibres take high axial tensile strain. As the ankle dorsiflexes, the posterosuperior calcaneus presses into the deep fibres and the retrocalcaneal bursa, causing high transverse compressive strain [r1]. Running loads the Achilles 4 to 6 times body weight [r1]. Compression is thought to drive fibrocartilaginous change and proteoglycan build-up in the tendon [r2].

name: Knee dislocation (multiligament knee injury)
populations: young adult males in high-energy trauma
summary: Disruption of two or more major knee ligaments, usually both cruciates, from high- or low-energy trauma. The knee may have spontaneously reduced; popliteal artery and peroneal nerve injury must be excluded.

keyFacts.label: Urgency
keyFacts.value: Emergency: limb-threatening popliteal artery injury in about 1 in 5

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Ankle–brachial index: <0.90 detected all arterial injuries in one prospective series

keyFacts.label: Nerve injury
keyFacts.value: Common peroneal nerve injury in about 25%

keyFacts.label: Classification
keyFacts.value: Schenck anatomic (KD-I to KD-V, with C and N modifiers)

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: 12–18 months; return to any sport about 54%, high-level sport 22–33%

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Radiographs, CT angiography if ABI <0.90 or abnormal pulses, then MRI

grading: Schenck anatomic classification of knee dislocation (Wascher modification)

keywords.mechanism: Dislocation needs disruption of most of the knee's restraints. High-energy mechanisms (vehicle crashes, falls from height) and sports collisions apply hyperextension, a posterior force on the flexed tibia, or combined varus/valgus with rotation. Hyperextension tends to produce anterior dislocation: the posterior capsule and PCL fail and the popliteal artery, tethered above and below the knee, is stretched. A dashboard blow to the flexed knee produces posterior dislocation, which has a high vascular injury rate [r2]. In people with obesity, a low-energy fall or misstep can dislocate the knee [r6].

name: Lateral ankle sprain
populations: people with a previous ankle sprain
recreational walkers and runners on uneven ground
summary: A partial or complete tear of the lateral ankle ligaments, usually the ATFL first, from a sudden inversion and internal-rotation roll of the foot on landing, cutting or uneven ground.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Pain falls quickly over the first 2 weeks, but 5–33% still report pain at 1 year

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based; no validated criteria exist. Often weeks for mild–moderate sprains (clinical convention)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Delayed physical examination at 4–5 days (Sn 96%, Sp 84% for ligament rupture); Ottawa ankle rules exclude fracture (Sn 99.4%)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not routine; radiographs only when the Ottawa ankle rules are positive

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Incidence is highest in children, then adolescents, then adults (2.85, 1.94 and 0.72 per 1,000 exposures)

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Females 13.6 vs males 6.94 per 1,000 exposures; indoor and court sports carry the highest risk

grading: Clinical sprain grading (I–III; several variants are in use)

tests: Delayed physical examination (4–5 days after injury)
Syndesmosis screen (squeeze and external rotation tests)
structures: Talar dome and distal tibiofibular syndesmosis
keywords.mechanism: Lateral ankle sprains typically occur when the rearfoot undergoes excessive supination on an externally rotated lower leg [r2]. Analyses of real injuries show a sudden inversion with internal rotation of the foot shortly after landing. In five televised tennis cases, peak inversion ranged from 48° to 126° and peak internal rotation from 35° to 99°, with the foot only slightly inverted at the moment of landing [r3]. In a laboratory handball side-step, inversion and internal rotation peaked 130–180 ms after initial contact [r11]. The classic teaching of plantarflexion plus inversion is a useful simplification, but the sagittal-plane position was variable: the tennis cases fluctuated between plantarflexion and dorsiflexion in the first 0.5 s after foot strike [r3], and the handball case showed considerable dorsiflexion [r11].

name: Lateral elbow tendinopathy (tennis elbow)
summary: A load-related overuse tendinopathy of the common extensor origin (ECRB) at the lateral epicondyle, causing pain with gripping and wrist extension. Managed with education, load modification and progressive exercise.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Usually self-limiting, but symptoms can persist beyond 1 year in up to 20% of people

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based, not time-based: pain-free gripping and tolerance of full work or sport load; most people in trials were much improved by 6–12 months

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Tenderness at the lateral epicondyle plus pain on resisted wrist or middle-finger extension and gripping. In one small study (30 patients, all with the condition) sensitivity was 0.97 for Cozen's test and 0.87 for Mill's test

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not needed to make the diagnosis. In 21 patients MRI showed tendinosis signal in 18, but the severity of the signal did not match symptoms

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: 45–54 years in a Finnish population sample; equally common in men and women

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Prevalence of definite lateral epicondylitis 1.3% in adults aged 30–64; incidence fell from 4.5 to 2.4 per 1000 people between 2000 and 2012 in one US cohort

grading: Tendinopathy continuum (Cook and Purdam): a structural staging model, used alongside pain and function

tests: Palpation of the lateral epicondyle and ECRB origin
structures: Extensor carpi radialis longus and brachioradialis
Radial collateral and lateral ulnar collateral ligaments
Posterior interosseous nerve and arcade of Frohse
Capitellum, radial head and annular ligament
differentials: Posterolateral rotatory instability or lateral collateral ligament injury
Intra-articular pathology (synovial plica, osteoarthritis, loose body)
Referred pain from the shoulder or trigger points
keywords.mechanism: Lateral elbow tendinopathy has no single injury moment. It develops when repeated or sustained gripping and wrist extension load the common extensor origin faster than the tendon can adapt. During a grip the extensor carpi radialis brevis and its neighbours hold the wrist extended and stable while the finger flexors squeeze, so a heavy or repetitive grip (hammering, lifting, a racquet stroke, mouse work) transmits high tension to the origin at the lateral epicondyle [r2,r4]. When load repeatedly exceeds capacity, the tendon moves from a reactive state towards disrepair and degeneration [r9].

name: Lateral patellar dislocation
summary: The patella leaves the trochlear groove, almost always laterally, usually in a twisting knee injury. The medial patellofemoral ligament tears, and the patella often relocates on its own.

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: About 23 per 100,000 person-years overall; about 148 per 100,000 at age 14–18

keyFacts.label: Recurrence
keyFacts.value: Roughly 17–40% after a first dislocation, depending on risk factors, population and follow-up

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Medial patellar tenderness and patellar apprehension; no validated accuracy data identified

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Radiographs for fracture or loose body; MRI shows MPFL injury and bone bruises

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Rehabilitation over about 3–6 months; criteria-based, not time-based

keyFacts.label: Management
keyFacts.value: Most uncomplicated first dislocations are managed without surgery

grading: Clinical pattern of patellar instability (WARPS versus STAID)

structures: Medial patellomeniscal ligament and medial retinaculum
keywords.mechanism: The classic mechanism is a non-contact twisting injury. The foot is planted, the knee is flexed, and the femur rotates internally over the fixed tibia as the knee collapses into valgus. The quadriceps pull then drives the patella over the lateral trochlear ridge. A direct blow to the medial patella can also cause it. No mechanism-of-injury study was identified in the sources reviewed, so the sequence below is the standard clinical description. It fits the injury pattern on MRI: medial patellar restraint damage with bone bruises of the lateral femoral condyle and the medial patella [r4].

name: Lumbar disc herniation with radiculopathy
populations: people with heavy lifting or prolonged sitting exposure
summary: Displacement of disc material through a fissured annulus, usually posterolaterally at L4–5 or L5–S1, irritating a nerve root and causing leg-dominant pain. Most cases settle without surgery.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Most improve with non-surgical care; 95% of trial patients reported recovery at 1 year, with or without early surgery

keyFacts.label: Natural history
keyFacts.value: Herniations often resorb: pooled 70.4% overall, higher for extrusion and sequestration

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Straight leg raise (pooled sensitivity 0.92, specificity 0.28 in surgical samples); crossed SLR specificity 0.90

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI only if surgery or injection is planned, or red flags are present; protrusions are seen in 29–43% of pain-free adults

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: 30–50 years; male to female about 2:1

keyFacts.label: Red flag
keyFacts.value: Cauda equina syndrome is a same-day emergency

grading: Morphological classification of herniation (standard nomenclature)

keywords.mechanism: Repeated or sustained lumbar flexion combined with compressive load, often with some axial rotation, increases tensile strain on the posterior and posterolateral annulus while the nucleus is squeezed backwards. Cumulative loading creates annular fissures, the nucleus tracks outward along them and eventually pushes through the outer annulus toward the spinal canal or foramen, where it contacts a nerve root.

name: Medial collateral ligament (MCL) sprain
summary: A sprain or tear of the medial collateral ligament from a valgus force, usually a blow to the outside of the knee. Most isolated tears, even complete ones, heal well with early functional rehabilitation.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Grade I ~2 weeks; grade II 3–4 weeks; grade III 6–8+ weeks

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Mean lay-off 23 days in professional football

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Valgus stress at 30° (pain and laxity together: LR+ 6.4 with history)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Usually clinical; MRI if laxity in extension or suspected ACL, meniscal or posteromedial injury

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: ~70% contact: a blow to the lateral knee

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Most common knee ligament injury in professional football

grading: Clinical grading (valgus stress at 30° flexion, opening compared with the other side)

tests: Valgus stress test in full extension
structures: Deep MCL and posterior oblique ligament
keywords.mechanism: The typical mechanism is a valgus force: a blow to the lateral side of the knee, or a fall or tackle onto it, with the foot planted and the knee slightly flexed (about 20–30°), where the superficial MCL is the dominant restraint [r1,r4]. External rotation of the tibia often accompanies the valgus load and adds stress to the deep MCL and posteromedial structures. Non-contact valgus-rotation injuries (cutting, skiing) also occur, and higher-energy or more extended-knee injuries may involve the ACL [r1].

name: Medial elbow tendinopathy (golfer's elbow)
summary: A load-related overuse tendinopathy of the common flexor–pronator origin at the medial epicondyle, causing pain with wrist flexion, forearm pronation and gripping. Managed with education, load change and exercise.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Responds well to non-operative care in most people. In 20 refractory patients given eccentric exercise plus other measures, treatment lasted about 6 weeks on average (uncontrolled)

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based, not time-based: pain-free gripping, pronation and full swing or throwing load; in a surgical series 9 of 30 elbows needed more than 6 months to reach maximum improvement

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Tenderness at the medial epicondyle plus pain on resisted forearm pronation (positive in 28 of 30 elbows in a surgical series) or resisted wrist flexion (12 of 30)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not needed to make the diagnosis. Use it to exclude other causes, such as a UCL injury, an avulsion or a bony problem

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: 40–60 years; usually less common than lateral elbow tendinopathy

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Prevalence of definite medial epicondylitis 0.4% in Finnish adults aged 30–64, compared with 1.3% for lateral epicondylitis

grading: Tendinopathy continuum (Cook and Purdam): a structural staging model, used alongside pain and function [r10]

tests: Palpation of the medial epicondyle and common flexor origin
Passive wrist extension stretch (elbow extended, forearm supinated)
Valgus stress and moving valgus stress tests
Ulnar nerve screen (Tinel's sign and elbow flexion test)
structures: Pronator teres and flexor carpi radialis
Flexor carpi ulnaris and flexor digitorum superficialis
differentials: Posteromedial olecranon impingement or elbow osteoarthritis
keywords.mechanism: Medial elbow tendinopathy has no single injury moment. Flexor–pronator degeneration develops with repetitive forced wrist extension and forearm supination during activities that demand wrist flexion and forearm pronation, so the muscle group works eccentrically as the wrist is forced the other way and then concentrically to flex and pronate [r1]. In golf the trail arm flexes and pronates through impact; in throwing the load peaks in late cocking and early acceleration [r1]. When load repeatedly exceeds capacity the tendon moves from a reactive state towards disrepair and degeneration [r9].

name: Medial gastrocnemius strain ("tennis leg")
populations: people with a previous calf strain
summary: A strain of the medial gastrocnemius, usually at the musculotendinous junction, from a sudden push-off or lunge with the knee straightening while the ankle is dorsiflexed. It causes sharp calf pain and often a haematoma.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Mean return to play about 19 days for gastrocnemius strains (25 days for soleus) in elite Australian football; longer if severe

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based; running criteria are stricter than for other muscle strains, and recurrence is common

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Medial belly or musculotendinous tenderness, painful single-leg heel raise, and pain on stretch with the knee straight; exclude Achilles rupture (Thompson) and DVT

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not always needed. Ultrasound or MRI if the diagnosis is uncertain: medial gastrocnemius rupture in 67% of 141 'tennis leg' referrals

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Classically middle-aged recreational athletes; increasing age is one of the strongest risk factors

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Calf strains made up 3.6% of injuries over 5 years in one soccer study cited in a review

grading: Traditional clinical grading I–III (Dixon), with MRI-based alternatives: British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification (BAMIC) and the Munich consensus classification [r1,r8,r9]

tests: Palpation for medial belly and musculotendinous junction tenderness or a defect
Resisted plantarflexion and passive dorsiflexion, with the knee extended versus flexed
structures: Medial gastrocnemius (distal musculotendinous junction and aponeurosis)
differentials: Lumbar radiculopathy (S1) or other referred calf pain
keywords.mechanism: In the classic mechanism the knee extends while the ankle is dorsiflexed, as in a push-off from a lunge or an explosive start. This puts the biarticular medial gastrocnemius at its longest length just as it contracts hard [r1]. The muscle fails at its distal musculotendinous junction or aponeurosis, and blood tracks between the gastrocnemius and soleus. In an ultrasound series of 141 patients with a clinical diagnosis of tennis leg, the medial head was ruptured in 66.7% and the plantaris tendon in only 1.4% [r6].

name: Mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy
summary: A load-related overuse tendinopathy of the main body of the Achilles tendon, 2–6 cm above the heel, causing pain and stiffness with running and jumping. It is managed with progressive calf and tendon loading.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Months, not weeks: 12-week loading blocks improved symptoms in RCTs, and full recovery can take up to a year

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based graded return to running and jumping after a loading block; recurrence is common during the return phase

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Localised mid-portion thickening and tenderness; arc sign (pooled Sp 88%, Sn 42%) and Royal London Hospital test (+LR 3.84)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not needed to make the diagnosis; ultrasound or MRI if a tear or other pathology is suspected

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Active adults; mean age about 50 in the trials reviewed

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 1.85 per 1000 patients registered with Dutch GPs; a sport link was recorded in only 35% of cases

grading: Tendinopathy continuum (Cook and Purdam): a structural staging model, to be used alongside pain and function [r7,r10]

structures: Retrocalcaneal bursa and Kager's fat pad
keywords.mechanism: There is no single injury moment. In running, the Achilles tendon is stretched as the ankle dorsiflexes over the planted foot, then recoils as the calf drives the ankle into plantarflexion at toe-off. Each cycle loads the tendon several times body weight, and thousands of cycles are repeated per run. When load rises faster than the tendon's capacity, or recovery between sessions is too short, the mid-portion matrix cannot keep up and becomes painful and thickened (general biomechanics; no single source).

name: Olecranon bursitis
populations: manual workers who lean on their elbows
people with gout or rheumatoid arthritis
people on steroid therapy or with alcohol misuse (septic risk)
summary: Inflammation and fluid in the subcutaneous olecranon bursa from pressure, friction, a direct blow, crystal disease or infection. Aseptic cases usually settle with conservative care; septic bursitis needs same-day review.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: In a 90-patient trial of non-septic bursitis, 83% treated with compression and NSAIDs had resolved by 4 weeks; time to resolution was about 2–3 weeks across groups

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based: swelling settled, full pain-free elbow movement and tolerance of padded contact; no standard time frame

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Fluctuant swelling over the olecranon with a painless, full range of elbow movement. In septic cases tenderness (88% vs 36%), erythema (83% vs 27%), warmth (84% vs 56%) and fever (38% vs 0%) were more common, but the findings overlap

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not needed for uncomplicated cases. Ultrasound helps to separate bursitis from cellulitis; radiographs after trauma or for spurs and fractures

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Adults, mostly men; mean age 52 years in a series of septic bursitis (80% male)

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 29 per 100,000 person-years in a military population, rising to 97 per 100,000 in combat roles

grading: Aetiological classification (septic versus aseptic; acute traumatic, chronic microtraumatic, chronic inflammatory) [r3]

tests: Inspection and palpation of the bursa for fluctuance and warmth
Ultrasound of the bursa and skin
differentials: Cellulitis over the elbow without bursitis
Gout or other crystal or inflammatory arthritis
Olecranon fracture or elbow injury after a fall
Elbow dislocation or other joint injury
Elbow joint effusion or inflammatory arthritis
keywords.mechanism: The olecranon bursa is a thin sac between the point of the elbow and the skin. It reduces friction between them, and when the skin is repeatedly pressed or slid against bone the bursal lining becomes irritated and fills with fluid. The same bursa can be injured by a single direct blow, which causes bleeding into it, or inoculated with bacteria through broken skin [r3,r5]. Chronic microtrauma is the most common cause of superficial bursitis [r3].

name: Osgood–Schlatter disease
aka: traction apophysitis of the tibial tubercle
summary: A traction apophysitis of the tibial tuberosity in growing adolescents. Repeated quadriceps pull through the patellar tendon causes activity-related pain below the knee. Usually self-limiting, but it can persist.

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Up to about 10% of adolescents; higher in sports-active adolescents

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Boys 12–15 years, girls 8–12 years (older estimates); sex difference may be shrinking

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Tenderness and a prominence over the tibial tuberosity; pain on resisted knee extension and kneeling. Clinical diagnosis

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not usually needed; lateral radiograph or ultrasound if atypical

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Self-limiting with physeal closure, but adolescents in one cohort had pain for a mean of 21 months before enrolling

keyFacts.label: Management
keyFacts.value: Education, load management and progressive strengthening. 80% reported success at 12 weeks in a case series

grading: Radiographic progression (descriptive; no validated clinical grading)

tests: Kneeling or direct pressure over the tuberosity
structures: Infrapatellar fat pad and deep infrapatellar bursa
differentials: Hip pathology referring to the knee (for example slipped capital femoral epiphysis)
keywords.mechanism: OSD has no single injury moment. Jumping, sprinting, kicking and landing load the quadriceps repeatedly, and each contraction pulls through the patella and patellar tendon onto the tibial tuberosity. During growth that attachment is on a secondary ossification centre rather than mature bone, so it is the weak link [r1,r4]. Repetitive traction produces microtrauma and irritation at the apophysis. Radiographs show irregularity and separation of the apophysis early on, and fragmentation later [r1]. The apophysis fuses as growth finishes, and most symptoms settle [r1,r3].

name: Osteochondritis dissecans (OCD) of the knee
summary: A focal disorder of subchondral bone, usually on the lateral side of the medial femoral condyle in active adolescents, that can loosen the overlying cartilage and bone. Stable juvenile lesions often heal with offloading.

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: 12–19 years; about 4 times more common in males

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 9.5 per 100,000 in 6–19-year-olds

keyFacts.label: Typical site
keyFacts.value: Medial femoral condyle (64%), classically its lateral aspect

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Radiographs including a notch (tunnel) view; MRI to assess size and stability

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Stable juvenile lesions: about two-thirds progress to healing in 6 months of offloading

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: No reliable clinical test; diagnosis is radiological

grading: Stability and skeletal maturity, with the ROCK arthroscopic classification

keywords.mechanism: There is usually no single injury. Repetitive impact and shear load the subchondral bone of the femoral condyle faster than it can remodel, particularly in adolescents whose secondary ossification centre is still maturing. One theory is that the tibial spine impinges on the lateral aspect of the medial femoral condyle when the tibia rotates internally. The bone beneath the cartilage weakens, becomes ischaemic and separates from the parent bone, and the cartilage may then fissure and detach [r3].

name: Patella fracture
summary: A fracture of the kneecap from a direct blow (fall onto the knee, dashboard) or a sudden eccentric quadriceps contraction. Displaced fractures disrupt the extensor mechanism and usually need fixation.

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: About 13 per 100,000 per year; highest in women aged 60–80

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Active straight-leg raise: inability suggests extensor mechanism disruption

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: AP, lateral and skyline radiographs; Ottawa rules include isolated patellar tenderness

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Bone union ~6–8 weeks; strength and function 6–12 months

keyFacts.label: Surgery threshold
keyFacts.value: Extensor mechanism disrupted, or >2–3 mm step-off / >1–4 mm displacement

keyFacts.label: Common complication
keyFacts.value: Symptomatic implant removal in about 30% after fixation

grading: Descriptive classification by pattern and displacement (AO/OTA 34)

tests: Active straight-leg raise / extensor lag test
keywords.mechanism: Two mechanisms dominate [r2]. A direct blow to the front of the flexed knee, typically a fall onto a hard surface or a dashboard impact, compresses the patella against the femoral trochlea and tends to produce comminuted (stellate) fractures, often with the retinacula intact. An indirect mechanism, a sudden eccentric quadriceps contraction while the knee is flexed (for example, stumbling and trying to stop a fall), loads the patella in tension like a beam over the trochlea and produces a transverse fracture whose fragments are pulled apart when the medial and lateral retinacula also tear. Many falls combine both.

name: Patellar tendinopathy (jumper's knee)
summary: A load-related overuse tendinopathy of the proximal patellar tendon, causing pain at the base of the kneecap with jumping, landing and deceleration. It is managed with progressive tendon loading.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Months, not weeks: in a 24-week trial, VISA-P improved by 28 points with progressive loading (18 with eccentric exercise)

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based. In a chronic, mostly previously treated cohort, 43% (progressive loading) and 27% (eccentric) had returned in the 24-week trial

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Load-related pain at the inferior pole of the patella; single-leg decline squat reproduces it. Palpation PPV 68% in symptomatic tendons

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Ultrasound or MRI show tendon change but correlate poorly with symptoms; not needed to make the diagnosis

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Young athletic adults (mean age 24 in the main RCT); more common in men

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Prevalence 14.2% in elite athletes across sports; 44.6% in elite volleyball

grading: Tendinopathy continuum (Cook and Purdam): a structural staging model, to be used alongside pain and function [r3]

tests: Palpation of the patellar tendon at the inferior pole
differentials: Patellar tendon rupture or partial tear
keywords.mechanism: Patellar tendinopathy has no single injury moment. It develops from repeated high loading of the knee extensor mechanism in the stretch–shortening cycle. On landing or deceleration the quadriceps contracts eccentrically as the hip, knee and ankle flex, so the patellar tendon lengthens and stores elastic energy; on take-off or push-off it recoils and returns that energy [r1]. When this loading is repeated faster than the tendon can adapt, load exceeds capacity and the tendon's structure changes [r2]. Landing strategy matters: in drop jumps, athletes with previous jumper's knee landed more stiffly, with higher knee angular velocity and loading rates [r8].

name: Patellofemoral pain
summary: Pain around or behind the kneecap, provoked by squatting, stairs or running, which arises when repeated patellofemoral load exceeds tissue capacity. Managed with education and hip-plus-knee exercise.

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Anterior knee pain on squatting (PFP present in about 80% of people positive); there is no definitive test

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Education plus a physical treatment beats wait-and-see at 3 months, but many people still have symptoms years later

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based, with modified activity usually continued throughout rehab

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not needed to diagnose; structural findings correlate imprecisely with pain

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Adolescents and young adults; common in female athletes, runners and military recruits

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Annual prevalence 22.7% in the general population and 28.9% in adolescents (systematic review)

tests: Single-leg squat / step-down with movement analysis
Clarke's (patellar grinding) test and apprehension test
structures: Hip abductors, external rotators and foot–ankle complex
keywords.mechanism: There is no single injury event. PFP develops when repeated or suddenly increased patellofemoral joint load, usually through a flexed, weight-bearing knee (mid-stance of running, stair ascent or descent, squatting, jump landings), exceeds the capacity of the joint's tissues [r3]. As the knee bends under load, the quadriceps must produce more force to control the flexion moment, and that force and the patellar tendon pull compress the patella into the trochlear groove. Hip adduction and knee abduction (valgus) during running and landing are associated with PFP, although prospective evidence is limited and inconsistent [r8,r9].

name: Posterior ankle impingement
populations: people with an os trigonum or a prominent lateral talar process
summary: Posterior ankle pain in forced plantarflexion as the posterior talar process or os trigonum, capsule and soft tissue are squeezed between the tibia and calcaneus, typical in dancers and footballers.

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Forced or repeated plantarflexion: en pointe or demi-pointe, kicking, push-off, downhill running

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Most improve with non-surgical care; in one small series 60% improved without surgery and 40% needed excision

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Posterior pain reproduced by forced passive plantarflexion; diagnosis is mainly clinical

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Lateral radiograph in maximal plantarflexion shows an os trigonum or posterior process; MRI shows soft tissue and oedema

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based. Full activity after arthroscopic excision averaged 11.3 weeks versus 16.0 weeks after open surgery

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: No population estimate found; dance accounts for 62% of sports cases reported in one review

grading: Descriptive classification by dominant pathology (no validated grading)

tests: Forced passive plantarflexion test (posterior impingement test)
Resisted great-toe flexion with the ankle plantarflexed (FHL test)
structures: Posterior talar process (lateral tubercle) and os trigonum
Os trigonum or posterior talar process
differentials: Flexor hallucis longus tendinopathy or tenosynovitis
keywords.mechanism: Forced plantarflexion closes the gap between the back of the tibia and the top of the calcaneus. In dancers en pointe, MRI showed the posterior edge of the tibial plafond, the posterior talus and the superior calcaneus converging in all nine dancers scanned [r7]. The posterior talar process, an os trigonum if present, and the soft tissue behind them are compressed between these bones [r2,r3]. Repeated loading in dancers, footballers and downhill runners, or a single hyperplantarflexion or inversion–plantarflexion injury, produces pain, swelling and sometimes fracture [r5,r1].

name: Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) injury
populations: motor vehicle and motorcycle trauma patients
summary: A partial or complete tear of the PCL from a posteriorly directed force on the proximal tibia with the knee flexed, such as a dashboard impact or a fall onto a bent knee with the foot pointed.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Isolated grade I–II: usually back to sport within 2–3 months; reconstruction 9–12 months

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Dashboard impact (~35%) or fall on the flexed knee with foot plantarflexed (~24%)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Posterior drawer with tibial step-off (Sn 90%, Sp 99% in chronic isolated tears)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI for acute injury; posterior stress radiographs quantify laxity (>8 mm suggests complete tear, >12 mm combined injury)

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Mid-20s to early 30s

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Up to 38% of acute knee haemarthroses in trauma centres; mostly combined injuries

grading: Clinical grading of posterior laxity (posterior drawer at 90° flexion, tibial step-off)

tests: Dial test (tibial external rotation) at 30° and 90°
structures: Posterior cruciate ligament (anterolateral and posteromedial bundles)
Posterolateral corner (LCL, popliteus tendon, popliteofibular ligament)
keywords.mechanism: The classic mechanism is a posteriorly directed force on the anterior proximal tibia while the knee is flexed to about 90°.
