This happens when the tibia strikes the dashboard in a car crash, or when an athlete falls forward onto a flexed knee with the ankle plantarflexed so that the tibial tuberosity, rather than the patella, takes the impact [r3]. The tibia is driven backward in the sagittal plane and the PCL, which is tight in flexion, fails. Hyperflexion and hyperextension are less common mechanisms; hyperextension and varus-rotation mechanisms often injure the posterolateral corner as well [r1].

name: Posterolateral corner (LCL/PLC) injury
summary: Injury to the lateral collateral ligament, popliteus tendon and popliteofibular ligament from a varus, hyperextension or external rotation force. Usually combined with cruciate injury; easily missed.

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Varus stress at 0° and 30°; dial test at 30° and 90°

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI; varus stress radiographs (>4 mm side-to-side suggests grade III)

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 9.1% of acute knee haemarthroses; 87% are combined injuries

keyFacts.label: Nerve risk
keyFacts.value: Common peroneal nerve injury in about one in four operated PLC injuries

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Grade I–II: 6–12 weeks; grade III reconstruction: 9–12 months

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Blow to the anteromedial knee in extension (hyperextension–varus)

grading: Clinical grading of varus/rotational laxity (with varus stress radiographs)

tests: Dial test (tibial external rotation at 30° and 90°)
structures: Medial femoral condyle and tibial plateau
keywords.mechanism: The classic mechanism is a posterolaterally directed blow to the anteromedial proximal tibia with the knee in or near full extension, which forces hyperextension and varus [r3]. Non-contact hyperextension–varus (landing or stepping awkwardly), and forced external rotation of the tibia on a flexed knee, also cause PLC injury. The force opens the lateral compartment in the frontal plane while the tibia rotates externally, and the medial compartment is compressed: an anteromedial femoral condyle bone bruise is a common MRI marker of this mechanism [r6].

name: Prepatellar bursitis
populations: tradespeople who kneel (tilers, carpet and floor layers, plumbers)
summary: Inflammation and swelling of the bursa in front of the kneecap from repeated kneeling, a blow or infection. About a third of cases are septic and need aspiration-guided antibiotic treatment.

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: At least 10 per 100,000 per year (with olecranon bursitis); 80% male, aged 40–60

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Repetitive kneeling, a direct blow or fall onto the patella, or skin breach

keyFacts.label: Septic
keyFacts.value: About one-third of cases; Staphylococcus aureus causes about 80%

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Bursal aspirate (cell count, Gram stain, culture, crystals) separates septic from non-septic

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Ultrasound confirms a bursal collection and helps distinguish cellulitis

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Non-septic: 2–6 weeks with protection from kneeling

grading: Aetiological classification

keywords.mechanism: The bursa is compressed between the floor and the patella with every kneel, and shear between skin and bone irritates its synovial lining. Repeated microtrauma (chronic kneeling) provokes inflammation and fluid production. A direct blow causes bleeding into the bursa (haemorrhagic bursitis). Because the bursa lies just under the skin, an abrasion or puncture can introduce bacteria, usually Staphylococcus aureus, causing septic bursitis [r1,r6].

name: Pubic-related groin pain (osteitis pubis)
summary: Longstanding groin pain from the pubic symphysis and adjacent pubic bone, best understood as a bone stress response to repetitive shear, with local symphyseal tenderness and often pubic bone marrow oedema on MRI.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Often 3–6 months; slower than other groin entities

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: 89% returned the next season after 12 weeks' unloading, but only 41% were symptom-free

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Local tenderness of the pubic symphysis and immediately adjacent bone

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI: pubic bone marrow oedema (also common in pain-free footballers)

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Least common Doha entity in a groin clinic (4%)

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Repetitive shear across the symphysis from kicking, running and cutting

tests: Single-leg hop / single-leg stance pain test
structures: Adductor longus and rectus abdominis entheses
keywords.mechanism: The pubic symphysis transmits load between the two halves of the pelvis. In single-leg stance during running and kicking, the stance-side pubis is driven upward by ground-reaction force while the swing side drops, creating vertical shear and rotation across the symphysis. At the same time the adductors pull the pubic bodies downward and laterally, and the rectus abdominis pulls them upward [r8]. Repetitive cyclical load without adequate recovery produces a bone stress response in the subchondral pubic bone (marrow oedema) and degeneration of the symphyseal disc and margins [r3,r9].

name: Rotator cuff related shoulder pain (subacromial pain)
populations: people returning to activity after a lay-off
summary: Activity-related shoulder pain with a painful arc, from load exceeding the capacity of the rotator cuff tendons. 'Impingement' as a purely mechanical explanation is contested.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Usually months of progressive loading; symptoms can persist or recur

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based, commonly about 3–6 months for overhead athletes (clinical convention)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Cluster of findings: painful arc, pain on resisted tests, Hawkins–Kennedy and Neer (no single test is diagnostic)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not routine; ultrasound if no improvement after about 6 weeks or a full-thickness tear is suspected

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: About 50 years (peak consultation incidence for shoulder conditions)

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 1.47% of UK adults consult yearly for any shoulder condition

tests: External rotation lag sign and drop-arm sign
structures: Supraspinatus tendon (critical zone near the footprint)
differentials: Internal impingement in the overhead athlete
keywords.mechanism: RCRSP usually develops gradually when the demands placed on the cuff tendons and subacromial tissues exceed their capacity, often after a change in overhead activity, a period of inactivity or a minor strain. Pain is typically provoked during loaded elevation, classically between about 60° and 120° of abduction (the painful arc, a clinical convention). The idea that the tendon is squeezed beneath the acromion is contested [r3,r1].

name: Scaphoid fracture
populations: athletes in contact and ball sports
people after a fall on an outstretched hand
summary: A break of the scaphoid, usually at the waist, from a fall on an outstretched hand with the wrist extended and radially deviated. Snuffbox tenderness needs imaging, as missed fractures risk nonunion and AVN.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Cast immobilisation for undisplaced waist fractures, then rehabilitation; trial outcomes are measured at 52 weeks (SWIFFT)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Snuffbox tenderness is sensitive (0.87–1.00 across studies) but not specific (0.03–0.98); combining tests raises specificity

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Radiographs can miss fractures; in a meta-analysis MRI had sensitivity 94.2% and specificity 97.7%, CT 81.5% and 96.0%

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Young adults; mean age 33 and 83% men in the SWIFFT trial

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 29 per 100,000 per year in a one-year Edinburgh study of radiographically confirmed fractures

keyFacts.label: Key risk
keyFacts.value: Blood enters the scaphoid mainly at the distal end, so proximal pole fractures risk avascular necrosis and nonunion

grading: Herbert classification (clinical convention) with a displacement threshold of 2 mm

structures: Scaphoid waist (most commonly) and proximal pole
Scapholunate ligament and other carpal ligaments
Soft tissues and radial wrist tendons
differentials: Thumb ulnar collateral ligament injury (skier's thumb)
keywords.mechanism: Most scaphoid fractures follow a fall on an outstretched hand in which the wrist is forced into extension and radial deviation. The scaphoid, which spans the proximal and distal carpal rows, is compressed between the radius and the distal row and then bent over the radial styloid. It fails at its narrowest part, the waist, and the fracture line usually runs obliquely or transversely across the bone (clinical biomechanics). The commonest pattern in a prospective series was a complete waist fracture [r2].

name: Sinding-Larsen–Johansson syndrome
summary: A traction apophysitis at the inferior pole of the patella in active adolescents. It causes activity-related pain at the lower kneecap and usually settles with load modification, though the evidence is limited.

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Uncommon: about 0.8% of 12–15-year-olds had MRI features in one cohort; quoted rates of 2–5% come from a case report

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Mainly physically active adolescents aged 9–17 years, more often boys

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Focal tenderness at the inferior pole of the patella with a normal straight-leg raise; no validated test accuracy data

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Radiographs may be normal early; ultrasound or MRI is the most useful. Exclude patellar sleeve fracture

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Conservative care reported to give positive outcomes within about 2–8 months; evidence is mostly case reports

keyFacts.label: Management
keyFacts.value: Education, load management and progressive exercise (extrapolated from Osgood–Schlatter disease)

tests: Palpation of the inferior pole of the patella
differentials: Bipartite patella or other normal variant
keywords.mechanism: SLJ is a traction injury. Repeated quadriceps contraction in jumping, running and kicking pulls the patella proximally, and the patellar tendon holds the inferior pole of the patella. The tendon attachment on the growing inferior pole is the weak link, so the tendon is loaded at its proximal attachment, which can be partially avulsed, with de novo calcification [r1]. The condition is attributed to repeated microtrauma [r10]. It usually lacks a single injury event, although an acute presentation after a non-contact jump or kick has been reported [r11,r5].

name: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE)
populations: children and adolescents aged about 8–15 years
children with endocrine disorders (hypothyroidism, growth hormone treatment)
summary: The femoral head (capital epiphysis) slips off the femoral neck through the growth plate in an adolescent, often presenting as a limp with thigh or knee pain. Same-day referral and non-weight-bearing are needed.

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: About 8–15 years, during the adolescent growth spurt

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: About 10.8 per 100,000 children

keyFacts.label: Key sign
keyFacts.value: Hip held in external rotation as it is flexed, with reduced internal rotation

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Both hips: AP plus frog-leg (stable) or cross-table lateral (unstable) radiographs

keyFacts.label: Stability
keyFacts.value: Unstable slips (cannot bear weight) had 47% AVN vs 0% in stable slips

keyFacts.label: Pitfall
keyFacts.value: Knee or thigh pain doubles the diagnostic delay; always examine the hip

grading: Loder stability classification (with slip-angle severity)

keywords.mechanism: SCFE is a mechanical failure of the proximal femoral physis under shear. During the growth spurt the physis is thicker and its hypertrophic zone weaker; excess body weight raises the shear force across it, and a more vertical physis or retroverted femoral neck increases that shear [r1,r10]. The physis gradually gives way (stable slip) or fails suddenly after minor trauma (unstable slip). The epiphysis stays in the acetabulum while the neck displaces anteriorly and rotates externally.

name: Spondylolysis (pars stress fracture)
summary: A fatigue (stress) fracture of the pars interarticularis, most often at L5, from repetitive lumbar extension and rotation in adolescent athletes. Early-stage lesions can heal, so prompt diagnosis matters.

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Adolescent athletes: 47% of 100 adolescent athletes with back pain had spondylolysis, versus 5% of adults with acute low back pain

keyFacts.label: Prevalence
keyFacts.value: 5.9% of the Japanese general population on CT (90% at L5); 8.0% of Spanish elite athletes, up to 26.7% in throwing sports

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: No physical test is diagnostic; the one-legged hyperextension test was not supported (sensitivity 50–73%, specificity 0–87%)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI found active spondylolysis missed by radiographs in 48.5% of 200 young athletes; SPECT or CT is more sensitive but uses radiation

keyFacts.label: Healing
keyFacts.value: Union with a hard brace: 94% early, 64% and 27% progressive (high and low MRI signal), 0% terminal defects

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Median 2.5 months (75 days) to return to sport in one 12-athlete functional progression series

grading: CT stage (early, progressive, terminal) with STIR MRI subdivision of progressive defects

differentials: Other bone stress injury or apophyseal ring injury
Infection, tumour or inflammatory back pain
keywords.mechanism: Repetitive lumbar extension combined with rotation, and torsion against resistance, loads the pars interarticularis of the lower lumbar vertebrae, most often L5, until bone microdamage outpaces repair [r1,r4]. The lesion progresses from a bone stress reaction with marrow oedema to an incomplete and then a complete stress fracture; early lesions can heal, while terminal lesions form a non-union [r9,r10].

name: Tibial plateau fracture
summary: An intra-articular fracture of the proximal tibia caused by axial load combined with valgus or varus, from a low-energy fall in older adults or high-energy trauma. Compartment syndrome and soft tissue injury are common.

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: About 10 per 100,000 per year; peaks at 40–60 years

keyFacts.label: Classification
keyFacts.value: Schatzker I–VI (lateral split → bicondylar)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Ottawa knee rules to trigger radiographs (Sn 0.99)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Radiographs then CT for fracture planning; MRI shows soft tissue injury

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Protected weight-bearing 6–12 weeks; return to sport ~7 months or longer

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: About 70% return overall

grading: Schatzker classification

structures: Leg compartments and common peroneal nerve
keywords.mechanism: Most plateau fractures result from an axial load through the extended or slightly flexed knee combined with a valgus (or, less often, varus) force. The femoral condyle acts like a hammer on the plateau below it: valgus drives the lateral femoral condyle into the lateral plateau, splitting the cortex and depressing the articular surface. In dense young bone the plateau tends to split; in osteoporotic bone it tends to depress. Varus loading produces medial plateau fractures, which are often higher energy and may be fracture-dislocations; pure high-energy axial loads produce bicondylar fractures [r2].

name: Traumatic hip dislocation
populations: young adult males in road traffic crashes
summary: The femoral head is forced out of the acetabulum, usually posteriorly when a flexed, adducted hip is driven backwards along the femur (dashboard injury). Reduction within 6 hours limits avascular necrosis.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Protected weight-bearing about 6–8 weeks; return to sport often 3–6 months if no AVN

keyFacts.label: Key priority
keyFacts.value: Emergency reduction: AVN risk rises sharply with delay (OR 5.6 if reduced after 12 h)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: AP pelvis, then post-reduction CT; MRI at about 6 weeks to screen for AVN

keyFacts.label: Direction
keyFacts.value: About 90% posterior: leg shortened, flexed, adducted and internally rotated

keyFacts.label: Nerve injury
keyFacts.value: About 10% of adults, mainly the sciatic (peroneal division)

keyFacts.label: Long-term
keyFacts.value: AVN and post-traumatic arthritis are common, especially with associated fractures

grading: Thompson–Epstein classification (posterior dislocation)

tests: Posterior apprehension (flexion–adduction–internal rotation with posterior load)
structures: Posterior capsule, ischiofemoral ligament, ligamentum teres
keywords.mechanism: Posterior dislocation occurs when an axial force travels along the femoral shaft with the hip flexed and adducted, as when the knee strikes a car dashboard. The force levers the femoral head over the posterior acetabular rim, tearing the posterior capsule and labrum. With less flexion or more abduction at impact, the posterior wall of the acetabulum fractures (fracture-dislocation) [r1,r2]. Anterior dislocation results from forced abduction and external rotation, with the hip extended (pubic type) or flexed (obturator type) [r2].

name: Traumatic meniscal tear
populations: people with an acute ACL injury
manual workers who squat and twist
summary: An acute tear of the medial or lateral meniscus from twisting on a flexed, weight-bearing knee, causing joint-line pain, delayed swelling and sometimes catching or locking.

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Weight-bearing knee flexion with rotation on a planted foot

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Joint-line tenderness (Sn 83%, Sp 83%); Thessaly 20° (Sn 75%, Sp 87%)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI when surgery is being considered or the knee locks

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Mean ~2 months after partial meniscectomy; ~6 months after repair

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Exercise-first care: clinically relevant improvement by 12 weeks to 12 months

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Adolescents and adults under 40 in pivoting sport

grading: Tear pattern and vascular zone (arthroscopic/MRI description)

keywords.mechanism: The classic non-contact mechanism is rotation of the femur on a fixed tibia while the knee is flexed and loaded, for example twisting to change direction with the foot planted. Axial compression traps the meniscus between the femoral condyle and tibial plateau while rotation and anteroposterior translation shear it. The posterior horn of the medial meniscus is least mobile and is the usual site; the lateral meniscus is more often torn at the time of an acute ACL rupture.

name: Traumatic rotator cuff tear
populations: adults in their 50s (mean about 55 years in one systematic review)
older adults after a fall or shoulder dislocation
summary: A sudden tear of one or more rotator cuff tendons after a fall or forceful pull, with immediate pain and weakness. It may be a new tear or an acute-on-chronic extension of a degenerate tendon.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Months: about 6–12 months after repair (clinical convention); non-operative recovery is slower and less predictable for large tears

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based; commonly not before about 6 months after repair, and 9–12 months for overhead or contact sport (clinical convention)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: External rotation lag sign (LR+ 7.2) and internal rotation lag sign (LR+ 5.6) for full-thickness tears

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Ultrasound or MRI: sensitivity and specificity over 0.90 for full-thickness tears

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Mean about 55 years (systematic review of traumatic tears), largely male

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: Fall onto the arm most common; subscapularis involved in 78% in the same review

grading: Descriptive classification by depth and size (no single universally accepted system)

structures: Rotator interval and long head of biceps
Long head of biceps and rotator interval
keywords.mechanism: A traumatic tear usually follows a fall onto the outstretched or abducted arm, or a sudden forceful pull, in which the cuff tendons are overloaded eccentrically while the arm is abducted and externally rotated [r1]. The load exceeds the tensile capacity of the tendon, which is often already degenerate. The failure typically starts in the supraspinatus near its footprint on the greater tuberosity and can extend posteriorly to infraspinatus and anteriorly to the rotator interval and subscapularis.
